merges.description: Alexander Antonov (recorded in the INS files as Aleksandr Opotsky, and also as Antonoff) was born about 1896 in Grodno Province, Russia (present-day Belarus). He immigrated to the United States in 1913 and worked as a laborer. He joined the Union of Russian Workers in McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania in 1917, served as a delegate for the IWW’s General Recruiting Union in Pittsburgh, and identified himself as an anarchist. Arrested in Pittsburgh on April 14, 1919, he told interrogators “I believe in no government of any kind,” and instead “I favor the system of [Peter] Kropatkin [sic].” He was deported to Soviet Russia aboard the Buford on December 21, 1919. After reportedly being imprisoned in seventeen Soviet prisons, he emigrated to Argentina sometime before 1921 with help from comrades abroad. Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.
merges.note: Same Buford deportee — born Grodno 1896, URW and IWW in Pittsburgh, arrested April 1919, sailed December 21, 1919. The INS file name was Opotsky. The two bios each held detail the other lacked, so the survivor gets a composed biography carrying all of it, including the Kropotkin quote and the seventeen Soviet prisons.

merges.description: Robert Feehan, a Structural Iron Workers Industrial Union member from Chicago, Illinois, was convicted at the mass IWW trial and sentenced to four years in prison for conspiracy to violate federal statutes, including the Espionage Act. He served in Leavenworth Penitentiary from September 1918 to February 22, 1922. His case is documented in the National Civil Liberties Bureau’s March 1919 compilation “War-Time Prosecutions and Mob Violence”; a duplicate roster entry spelled the surname Freehan.
merges.note: Freehan is the corrupted spelling, but it carried the fuller biography, so the text moves onto the correctly spelled record — the same direction as Harrison George in batch 45.

merges.description_append: MacDonald was diagnosed with a mild case of tuberculosis, but the government refused to grant clemency because he had published the poem “A Patriot” in the Industrial Worker: “I love my country, yes, I do, / I love my Uncle Sam, / I also love my steak and eggs, / I guess I won’t enlist. / I love my flag, I do, I do, / Which floats upon the breeze, / I also love my arms, and legs, / I guess I won’t enlist. / I love my country, yes, I do, / I hope her folks do well; / Without our arms and legs and things / I think we’d look like Hell. / Yet men with faces half shot off / Are unfit to be seen; / I’ve read in books it spoils their looks, / I guess I won’t enlist.”
merges.note: The drop's name field reads 'Although MacDonald' — a corrupted import that split one profile mid-sentence. Its content, the tuberculosis clemency refusal and the full text of the poem A Patriot, is appended to the survivor's biography. Wrinkle preserved: the fragment says his sentence was commuted in October 1923, while the survivor's Zimmer text has him deported to Canada on August 5, 1923.

merges.description_append: Before the Chicago prosecution he was one of the 74 IWW members held in the Snohomish County jail and charged with murder after the Everett Massacre of November 5, 1916, when Sheriff Donald McRae and a posse of armed vigilantes opened fire on the steamer Verona at the Everett dock, killing at least five Wobblies. The charges against all 74 were dropped after Thomas H. Tracy’s acquittal on May 5, 1917. At the time of the massacre he was 56, a painter, born in Michigan.
merges.note: Two episodes of one man — the Everett Massacre detention and the Chicago-trial prosecution; the survivor's AKA already reads J. H. Byers. The Everett case row MOVES onto the survivor. THE TWO PHOTOS ARE NOT THE SAME PHOTOGRAPH AND NOT PLAUSIBLY THE SAME MAN: the survivor carried a Houghton Library studio cabinet card of a young man in a wing collar, while the drop carries a prison mugshot, no. 4914, of a man in his fifties — and the record says Beyer was 56 at the time of the massacre. The mugshot replaces the cabinet card, which stays on disk.
